facts: Mercury has a longer sunrise-to-sunrise day than its year: 176 Earth days versus 88.
At some locations on Mercury, the Sun briefly rises, sets, and rises again.
Mercury's craters honour artists and writers, including Dr. Seuss.
Mercury has almost no seasonal changes because it spins nearly upright.
The Sun would look over three times wider from Mercury than from Earth.
Mercury can reach 430°C by day and drop to about −180°C at night.
Mercury's enormous metal core occupies about 85% of the planet's radius.
Long cliffs on Mercury formed as its cooling interior contracted.
Bright streaks around Mercury's craters are crushed rock thrown out by impacts.
Mercury has no substantial atmosphere to hold onto daytime heat.
Venus turns so slowly that one rotation takes longer than one orbit around the Sun.
On Venus, the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east.
Venus is hotter than Mercury even though it is farther from the Sun.
The surface of Venus is hot enough to melt lead.
Venus's surface air pressure is roughly 93 times Earth's sea-level pressure.
The morning star and evening star can both be Venus, seen at different times.
Venus shows phases through a telescope, much like our Moon.
Most named surface features on Venus commemorate women.
Venus's cloud tops race around the planet in hurricane-force winds.
About 50 kilometres above Venus's surface, atmospheric pressure is similar to Earth's at sea level.
Earth is the only planet whose English name does not come from Greek or Roman mythology.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
Earth's seasons come from its tilted axis, not simply its changing distance from the Sun.
About 30 Earths could fit side by side between Earth and the Moon.
Earth occasionally captures small asteroids as temporary moons.
Our Moon helps stabilise Earth's axial wobble.
Earth's inner core is solid, while its surrounding outer core is liquid.
Earth's ocean crust is generally thinner than its continental crust.
Most of the air you breathe is nitrogen, not oxygen.
Measured from its submerged base, Mauna Kea is taller than Mount Everest.
Mars is red because iron-bearing minerals in its dust have rusted.
A Martian day is only about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day.
Mars has seasons, but they last longer and have less equal lengths than Earth's.
Mars's two small moons are lumpy because their gravity cannot pull them into spheres.
Phobos is spiralling toward Mars and may eventually break apart into a ring.
Mars has nearly as much surface area as all Earth's dry land combined.
Valles Marineris on Mars is a canyon system roughly as long as the continental United States is wide.
Olympus Mons on Mars has a base covering an area comparable to Arizona.
Evidence from Mars shows that today's desert planet once had a wetter, warmer past.
Deimos looks smoother than Phobos because loose material fills many of its craters.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm large enough to swallow Earth.
Jupiter spins once in about ten hours, giving it the shortest day of any planet.
Jupiter has faint rings that Voyager 1 discovered in 1979.
Jupiter's dark belts and bright zones carry winds in opposite directions.
Jupiter is about eleven times Earth's width.
Galileo spotted Jupiter's four largest moons with an early telescope in 1610.
Deep inside Jupiter, immense pressure makes hydrogen behave like an electrically conducting metal.
Juno's measurements suggest Jupiter has a partly dissolved, fuzzy core rather than a sharply bounded one.
Much of Jupiter's ring dust comes from impacts on its small inner moons.
Jupiter contains more mass than all the other planets combined.
Saturn's average density is lower than water's, unlike every other planet in our solar system.
Saturn's rings consist of countless separate pieces of ice and rock, not solid hoops.
Different parts of Saturn's rings orbit at different speeds.
Despite their enormous width, Saturn's main rings are typically only around ten metres thick.
Some chunks in Saturn's rings are as large as houses.
Saturn has seasons because its axis is tilted, much like Earth's.
A birthday on Saturn would come roughly once every 29 Earth years.
Saturn has no solid ground on which a visiting spacecraft could land.
Saturn's rings are lettered in discovery order, not in their order around the planet.
The Cassini Division is a gap thousands of kilometres wide between two of Saturn's main rings.
Uranus spins almost on its side, like a ball rolling around the Sun.
Parts of Uranus can endure roughly 21 Earth years of winter darkness.
Uranus's moons are named after characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.
William Herschel first mistook Uranus for a comet or star when he spotted it in 1781.
Herschel wanted to name Uranus after King George III.
Methane absorbs red light in Uranus's atmosphere, helping give it its blue-green colour.
Uranus is wider than Neptune but less massive.
Despite being called an ice giant, Uranus contains hot, dense fluids deep inside.
Some atmospheric regions on Uranus are colder than those on more distant Neptune.
Uranus has both dark inner rings and differently coloured outer rings.
Astronomers predicted Neptune's position from disturbances in Uranus's orbit before finding it.
Galileo recorded Neptune centuries before its discovery but mistook it for a star.
Neptune completed its first orbit since its 1846 discovery only in 2011.
Each season on Neptune lasts more than 40 Earth years.
Neptune's moon Triton orbits against the planet's rotation, suggesting it was captured.
Voyager 2 found icy geysers on Triton despite its extremely cold surface.
Pluto and Neptune avoid collisions because their orbits follow a repeating rhythm.
Noon on Neptune would look much dimmer than daylight on Earth.
Neptune's rings contain unusual clumps called arcs rather than evenly distributed dust everywhere.
Neptune's largest moon was discovered just seventeen days after the planet itself.
